newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian army in horrifying state, minister says.
newsitem.headline: Russian army in horrifying state, minister says.

text.p: Russia's armed forces are in such a "horrifying state" of decay that the reliability of its nuclear weapons system is in question, Defence Minister Igor Rodionov said.

Rodionov, firing the fiercest volley so far in a battle for military reforms and higher defence spending, said on Thursday he had set out some of his fears in a letter to President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
He told senior members of the Russian media that a lack of funds had hit morale, reduced combat readiness and badly affected the armed forces' command and control centres.
"No one today can guarantee the reliability of our control systems," Interfax news agecy quoted Rodionov as saying.
"Russia might soon reach the threshold beyond which its rockets and nuclear systems cannot be controlled."

Rodionov gave no details of his letter to Yeltsin. But in his comments to the Russian media representatives, he painted a picture of neglect of the nuclear arsenal and army which once contributed greatly to Moscow's superpower status.
His remarks signalled frustration at his inability to carry out the reforms he promised when Yeltsin appointed him last July.

Reforms appear to have failed to get off the drawing board partly because of differences over how to carry them out and also because of Yeltsin's absence form the Kremlin for much of the last seven months, delaying many major decisions.

"Reform in the armed forces has turned into a struggle for their survival, a struggle against disintegration," the 60-year-old minister, who recently left the army to become Russia's first civilian defence minister.
"The whole horror is in the fact that, as Russian defence minister, I am becoming a spectator of the destructive processes in the army and can nothing about it."

Rodionov said Russia's combat readiness had been dropping constantly since 1990 and its weapons systems were falling into decay while the United States, Moscow's former Cold War foe, was improving its own systems.
A shortage of satellites meant Russia's ability to track the nuclear forces of a potential enemy was deteriorating, while the United States observed Russia 24 hour a day, he said.
Ridionov was alarmed by the psychological condition of many soldiers, especially officers. The number of suicides in the military, once minimal, had risen to about 100 in 1996, he said.
"Uncontrollable processes, both in terms of hardware and servicemen, could develop with morale, and the psychological and material situation, the way it is," he said.
Many soldiers are underpaid, underfed and poorly clothed. The armed forces have not escaped the long wage delays affecting millions of employees across Russia.
A failure to boost spending, he said, would have a drastic effect.

"In such conditions, instead of the army being reformed by the year 2003 (As planned), we could lose it as a combat-capable entity, and this would mean the country completely loses its defensive capability," Rodionov said.
He was expected to give a joint news conference on Yeltsin's orders on Friday with Yuri Baturin, secretary of the Defence Council which is charged with overseeing military reforms.
Russian media say Rodionov and Baturin have clashed over their different visions of military reforms but the two men have played down the reports.
